The Teardown  /  01 Sept 2026

Issue 003  ·  4 min read  ·  1 file to install

Anthropic published a stage by stage account of how it builds software with coding agents. It travelled on one line, "code is no longer the bottleneck", which is the weakest part of the document.

The strongest part is one sentence about guardrails: a skill is advisory, a hook is the deterministic layer behind it. Any rule that has to hold without exception gets a hook. The rule Anthropic itself puts behind one is that the agent which wrote the code cannot approve it. Not a prompt asking the model to behave. A platform setting with no argument to win.

Here is ours. It is the file that has stopped every direct commit to main across this operation since July.

The file
.claude/hooks/git-flow-guard.mjs36 lines · node · no deps
#!/usr/bin/env node
// PreToolUse hook for Claude Code. Refuses `git commit` while the
// repo is on main or master. Exit 2 = the tool call is blocked and
// this message goes back to the agent. A merge in progress is the
// one legal commit on main (finishing a release or hotfix).
import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';

let raw = '';
process.stdin.on('data', (d) => (raw += d));
process.stdin.on('end', () => {
  let input;
  try { input = JSON.parse(raw); } catch { process.exit(0); }
  const cmd = String(input?.tool_input?.command ?? '');
  if (!/\bgit\b[^|&;\n]*\bcommit\b/.test(cmd)) process.exit(0);

  const dir = String(input?.cwd ?? process.cwd());
  const git = (args) => {
    try {
      const opt = { encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'ignore'] };
      return execFileSync('git', ['-C', dir, ...args], opt).trim();
    } catch { return null; }
  };

  const branch = git(['rev-parse', '--abbrev-ref', 'HEAD']);
  if (branch !== 'main' && branch !== 'master') process.exit(0);
  const merging = git(['rev-parse', '-q', '--verify', 'MERGE_HEAD']);
  if (merging !== null) process.exit(0);

  console.error(
    `git-flow-guard: BLOCKED. Direct commit on '${branch}' in ${dir}.\n` +
    'main takes code only by merging release/* or hotfix/* branches.\n' +
    'Feature: git checkout develop && git checkout -b feature/<name>\n' +
    'Urgent:  git checkout -b hotfix/<name>, commit there, merge back.'
  );
  process.exit(2);
});
What it stops

Any shell command containing git commit while the current branch is main or master. The hook exits with status 2, and the Claude Code docs are explicit that this is not negotiable: exit 2 blocks even if a JSON permissionDecision of allow is printed alongside it. The agent gets the message on stderr and does the sensible thing, which is to make a branch.

It is a brake, never a steering wheel. It cannot make the agent do anything, and it cannot make a commit good. What it can do is make one rule impossible to argue with, which turns out to be the only kind of rule an agent keeps.

What it cost us before

The rule existed before the hook did. It sat in bold, in the CLAUDE.md every session reads at startup, for four days. Sessions read it and committed on main anyway, because a rule in a prompt is a request, and a busy agent with a green test run treats a request as optional.

No rule, 4 days48Rule in CLAUDE.md, 4 days21Rule as a hook, 58 days4all in the first 3 hours

Direct commits on main, two repos, several Claude Code sessions a day. Rule written 2026-07-10, hook installed 2026-07-13. The four stragglers landed the night the hook went in, before the settings wiring did. Source: git log, read 2026-09-09.

Written down, the rule roughly halved the problem. As a hook it ended it. That gap is the whole argument for hooks, and it is the same shape as the number Anthropic's playbook never gives you.

Install in 2 minutes
  1. Save the file above as .claude/hooks/git-flow-guard.mjs. Put it in the folder above your repos and it covers every repo beneath, worktrees included.
  2. Register it in .claude/settings.json next to it:
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash|PowerShell",
      "hooks": [{ "type": "command",
                  "command": "node .claude/hooks/git-flow-guard.mjs" }]
    }]
  }
}
  1. Check out main, start Claude Code, ask it to commit anything. You should get the refusal back, and a branch. If you get a commit, the hook did not load: settings are read at session start, so restart the session.
The playbook, torn down

The reusable pattern in Anthropic's document is that every stage ends by committing a file, and that commit starts the next stage. Intent becomes intent.md, which triggers spec.md, then plan.md and the diff, then a reviewed PR, then an incident record that writes the next intent.md. The chain that produced a change and the audit trail for it are the same object. You never write the second one.

Stages, artifacts and the approval gate as described in the playbook. Source: Anthropic, The AI-Native SDLC Playbook, read at source 2026-09-07.

The premise underneath it is unsettled. The most careful study anyone has run, METR's randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 real tasks, forecast 24% faster and measured 19% slower, on early 2025 tooling. Read that as a warning about self assessment, not a verdict on agents. The file discipline does not need the premise to be true: if the agent is fast, the chain stops the speed turning into churn nobody can review, and if it is slow, you have lost some markdown.

Tried this week
Yesclaude --worktree <name>: one isolated checkout and branch per session, so two sessions stop stepping on each other's edits. Note that hooks in a parent folder are not isolated by it. The guard above is one of them, which is the point.
YesReading our own session transcripts (~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl) instead of guessing. Every message carries its token counts, so a cost claim can be checked against 103 real sessions before anyone runs an experiment. The number above came from git, not from memory.
One question

Which rule does your agent keep breaking, no matter how you word it?

Hit reply. One line is enough. I answer every reply, and the best one becomes next week's file.

If you only take one thing: a rule you cannot afford to have broken does not go in a prompt. It goes in a hook, and the prompt explains why.
